A close reading for the week

“Nelly, I am Heathcliff!”

Wuthering Heights · Chapter 9

Catherine has just agreed to marry Edgar Linton. Explaining herself to a housekeeper who does not want to listen, she gives one of the strangest accounts of love in Victorian fiction, and it is about existence, with pleasure left out.

“I cannot express it; but surely you and everybody have a notion that there is or should be an existence of yours beyond you.1 What were the use of my creation, if I were entirely contained here? … If all else perished, and he remained, I should still continue to be; and if all else remained, and he were annihilated, the universe would turn to a mighty stranger:2 I should not seem a part of it.

  1. 1

    A self stored elsewhere

    Catherine begins with a claim she says everyone secretly shares: that part of your existence is kept outside you, in another. It is nearer metaphysics than romance (she is arguing about what a person is, more than about what she feels), and her opening admission, “I cannot express it”, is honest. The whole speech is an attempt to express something the available language of love was not built for.

  2. 2

    The thought-experiment

    She tests the claim with annihilation: subtract everything but Heathcliff, and she persists; subtract Heathcliff, and the universe becomes “a mighty stranger”, still existing but no longer hers to belong to. The imagined loss is estrangement from the cosmos, something larger than grief. The novel holds her to this: after her death Heathcliff lives on in that estranged universe, begging her ghost to haunt him.
